How I work

My Design Process

My general approach to a design task. Each project shapes how much time each step needs.

  1. 01

    Understand

    Learn who the product is for and what they are trying to do before drawing anything.

  2. 02

    Define

    Turn what I learned into a clear problem and a short list of things the design has to solve.

  3. 03

    Explore

    Sketch flows and wireframes, try several directions and keep the simplest one that works.

  4. 04

    Design

    Build the interface with consistent type, spacing and components that hold up at every screen size.

  5. 05

    Prototype

    Connect the screens in Figma so the experience can be clicked through and judged as a whole.

  6. 06

    Refine

    Look for friction, take feedback and adjust the details until the flow feels clear.

About

About Lena

I'm a second-year student in the Computer Graphics Department at the National Polytechnic University of Armenia, studying by distance learning. I like the part of design where a messy idea becomes a screen that's easy to understand.

Alongside my studies I trained in UI/UX at Picsart Academy, where I designed a full mobile casino app, from research and personas to a design system and an interactive prototype. I'm especially interested in iGaming and gaming interfaces: clear deposits, readable bonuses and lobbies that put a player's favourite games first. I work mostly in Figma, FigJam and Adobe Photoshop, and I'm looking for a team where I can learn from real product work.

01

Overview

67 Casino is a mobile casino app I designed during the Picsart Academy design course. The project was created for educational purposes, to practise the full UI/UX process on one product: research, structure, wireframes, a design system, final screens and a prototype.

The name comes from the logo. It joins a chip-shaped 6 with a sharp, moving 7, a number many cultures see as lucky. Neon pink and a heavy italic typeface on a dark background give the brand a bold, playful tone.

02

Challenge

Casual players want to unwind, not fight the interface. Research and my persona, Marcus, a 29-year-old software engineer who plays in short evening sessions, pointed to three recurring problems: a cluttered game list that makes him search for the same favourites again and again, bonus and cashback terms that are hidden or confusing, and deposit flows that feel long and complicated.

The challenge was to design a mobile casino app that gets players to their favourite games fast, makes bonus progress easy to read and keeps deposits short and clear, all within a bold dark and neon brand.

03

Research

To understand the habits and needs of potential players, I ran an online survey in Google Forms: 10 multiple-choice questions, 16 respondents from the target audience of online casino and betting apps. It focused on lobby organisation, deposits, bonuses and navigation, and on whether a drag-and-drop favourites feature is in demand.

75%prefer a dark & neon look over a light one
75%most want to see favourite games on the Profile page
75%want to arrange their favourite games themselves

Insight → Design decision

Aesthetics

The strong preference for dark and neon confirmed the Deep Navy dark UI direction.

Information architecture

Favourite games mattered most, so that section is clearly visible at the top of the Profile and lobby.

Interaction

High interest in drag-and-drop made it the next feature to design and prototype.

04

User Flow

I mapped how a player moves through the app before designing screens. Everything starts from the lobby: signing up or logging in, then branching to search, categories, favourites, bonuses, profile and notifications. The deposit path runs from choosing an amount and payment method to a confirmed, updated balance.

05

Wireframes

Before any visual design I sketched low-fidelity wireframes for the main screens: sign-up and login, the lobby, search in two layout variants, and bonuses. Working without colour or imagery let me test layout, hierarchy and the central tab dock first.

06

Design System

  • Colour tokensPrimary pink for actions and highlights, with deep black, midnight black and pure white for surfaces and text.
  • Typography hierarchyA defined scale from display headings down to body and captions.
  • Components with statesBottom tab bar, primary and secondary buttons, segmented tabs, amount chips, form fields, game cards and promo banners.
  • Icon systemA consistent icon set drawn on a 24×24 grid for navigation and actions.
07

Design decisions

Each major decision traces back to the research: the survey, Marcus's persona and the competitor comparison.

  1. 1. Favourites first, and reorderable by the player

    Why. Marcus wants to arrange and reorder his favourite games himself, according to his mood, and he is frustrated by searching for the same games again and again. The survey agreed: 75% of respondents wanted to see their favourite games first, and 75% wanted to choose and arrange them themselves.

    In the design. A My Favourites shelf sits right under the bonus banner in the lobby. Players can long-press and drag to set their own order.

  2. 2. Dark and neon look

    Why. 75% of respondents preferred dark and neon over a light theme.

    In the design. A deep dark base with a single neon pink accent for actions and highlights, used across every screen through the design system.

  3. 3. Deposit on a single screen

    Why. Marcus finds deposits long and complicated, and in my comparison neither Stake nor 1xBet offered a fully single-screen deposit.

    In the design. Amount chips with a popular default, a visible minimum and maximum, and payment methods with their details up front, all above one Deposit button.

  4. 4. Bonuses that are easy to read and claim

    Why. Marcus distrusts bonus terms that are hidden or confusing, and in my comparison 1xBet had no structured bonus tracking or clear claim-to-active flow.

    In the design. Bonuses are split into Active, Available and Completed, and a Claim Now action moves a bonus from available to active. Notifications surface the same Claim Now card.

08

Final UI

Eight key screens of the app, in the order a player meets them: the logged-out lobby, creating an account, the lobby with the My Favourites shelf, search, deposit, profile, notifications and the game menu. Each one reuses the same tokens and components from the design system.

09

Prototype

The screens are connected in Figma so the experience can be clicked through from the lobby to account creation, search, bonuses, profile and deposit.

Open the Figma prototype ↗
10

Reflection

The hardest part was the survey. Collecting answers from many different people and bringing their opinions together was harder than I expected, because everyone wanted something a little different.

What I learned. This project taught me to understand people before designing for them. The survey showed that 75% of players wanted their favourite games first and wanted to arrange them themselves. That gave me a clear reason for the Favourites shelf, instead of relying on my own taste.

If I started again, I would move forward in clearer and simpler steps, so that each stage, from research to final screens, builds directly on the one before it.
